blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The covariance of two quantitative variables X and Y, measured on the same n individuals, is

cov(X, Y) = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ (n − 1)

The Pearson correlation coefficient r is the covariance divided by the product of the two standard deviations:

r = cov(X, Y) ÷ (sₓ × s_y) = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ √[Σ(x − x̄)² × Σ(y − ȳ)²]

It measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship and always lies between −1 and +1.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Covariance is the two-variable cousin of the variance (recall §3.6). The variance averages (x − x̄) × (x − x̄), a deviation times itself. Covariance averages (x − x̄) × (y − ȳ), one variable’s deviation times the other’s.

Look at the sign of each product. Draw a vertical line at x̄ and a horizontal line at ȳ (Figure 11.1). A child who is older and heavier than average sits in the upper right: plus × plus = plus. A child younger and lighter sits in the lower left: minus × minus = plus. Children in the other two corners give negative products. When most points fall in the two “plus” corners, the sum of products is large and positive. When the points spread evenly over all four corners, the products cancel and the covariance is near 0.

Covariance has awkward units (months × kg) and changes if you weigh in pounds. Dividing by sₓ × s_y removes the units. That is r.

blocks.alt: Sign of the cross-products for age and weight, 100 children
blocks.caption: Figure 11.1. Age against weight for the 100 children in the clinic register, with dashed lines at the two means. The 84 blue points lie in the two quadrants where (x − x̄)(y − ȳ) is positive; the 16 red points give negative products. The positive products dominate, so the covariance (9.38 kg × months) and r (0.82) are positive.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Why r cannot exceed 1 in size. Write each value as a z-score (recall §5.7.2.2.1): zₓ = (x − x̄)/sₓ and z_y = (y − ȳ)/s_y. Then:

  1. r = Σzₓz_y ÷ (n − 1): r is the average product of the two z-scores.
  2. Each set of z-scores has Σz² = n − 1, because Σ(x − x̄)² = (n − 1)sₓ².
  3. A sum of squares cannot be negative: Σ(zₓ − z_y)² ≥ 0.
  4. Expand: Σzₓ² + Σz_y² − 2Σzₓz_y = (n − 1) + (n − 1) − 2(n − 1)r = 2(n − 1)(1 − r) ≥ 0, so r ≤ 1.
  5. The same argument with Σ(zₓ + z_y)² ≥ 0 gives r ≥ −1.
  6. r = +1 only when every zₓ = z_y, that is, when all points lie exactly on a rising straight line.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
The first eight children to arrive at the clinic today had these heights (x, cm) and weights (y, kg):

Child 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
Height (cm) 80.5 78.5 96.2 74.4 89.9 96.4 85.5 86.4
Weight (kg) 11.2 9.8 14.1 10.0 12.3 13.6 11.1 11.9

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Use the computing forms Sₓᵧ = Σxy − (Σx)(Σy)/n, Sₓₓ = Σx² − (Σx)²/n and S_yy = Σy² − (Σy)²/n, which give the same sums of products and squares without subtracting a mean from each value.

  1. Totals: Σx = 687.8, Σy = 94.0, Σx² = 59,582.48, Σy² = 1,121.36, Σxy = 8,165.34; n = 8.
  2. Sₓᵧ = 8,165.34 − (687.8 × 94.0)/8 = 8,165.34 − 8,081.65 = 83.69.
  3. Sₓₓ = 59,582.48 − 687.8²/8 = 59,582.48 − 59,133.605 = 448.875. S_yy = 1,121.36 − 94.0²/8 = 1,121.36 − 1,104.50 = 16.86.
  4. Covariance = 83.69 ÷ 7 = 11.96 cm·kg. Every one of the eight products (x − x̄)(y − ȳ) is positive: each child is either taller and heavier, or shorter and lighter, than the average of the eight.
  5. r = 83.69 ÷ √(448.875 × 16.86) = 83.69 ÷ √7,568.0 = 83.69 ÷ 86.99 = 0.96.

Height and weight in these eight children lie close to a rising straight line. For all 100 children in the register, the covariance of age and weight is 9.38 kg·months, sₓ = 7.91 months and s_y = 1.45 kg, so r = 9.38 ÷ (7.91 × 1.45) = 9.38 ÷ 11.47 = 0.82.

Testing r and putting a confidence interval on it

The r of a sample estimates the population correlation ρ (rho). To test H₀: ρ = 0 (recall the steps of §8.7), use

t = r√(n − 2) ÷ √(1 − r²), with n − 2 degrees of freedom.

If both variables are Normally distributed, t follows the t-distribution on n − 2 degrees of freedom when ρ = 0 (R Core Team, documentation of R’s correlation test; derivation beyond this book, see Bland, 2015). Two degrees of freedom are lost because the same t tests whether the slope of the best-fitting straight line is zero (§12.2.4, the regression slope test), and fixing a straight line uses up two estimated quantities: its level (intercept) and its slope.

A confidence interval cannot be built as r ± 1.96 × SE, because r is trapped between −1 and +1 and its sampling distribution is skewed when ρ is far from 0. Fisher’s z-transformation fixes this (Fisher, 1915, derived the distribution of r):

z = ½ ln[(1 + r) ÷ (1 − r)], with SE(z) = 1 ÷ √(n − 3)

z is approximately Normal. Build the interval on the z scale and transform its ends back with r = (e²ᶻ − 1) ÷ (e²ᶻ + 1).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Eight children, r = 0.962: t = 0.962 × √6 ÷ √(1 − 0.9254) = 2.356 ÷ 0.273 = 8.63 on 6 df, p = 0.0001.
  2. Fisher z = ½ ln(1.962 ÷ 0.038) = 1.972. SE = 1 ÷ √5 = 0.447. 95% limits on the z scale: 1.972 ± 1.96 × 0.447 = 1.096 to 2.849. Back-transformed: 0.80 to 0.99.
  3. All 100 children, age and weight, r = 0.820: t = 0.820 × √98 ÷ √(1 − 0.673) = 8.119 ÷ 0.572 = 14.19 on 98 df, p < 0.001.
  4. z = ½ ln(1.820 ÷ 0.180) = 1.157. SE = 1 ÷ √97 = 0.102. Limits 1.157 ± 0.199 = 0.958 to 1.356. Back-transformed: 0.74 to 0.88.

The small sample gives a wide interval (0.80 to 0.99) even though its r is higher. The interval is not symmetric about r: the upper limit cannot pass 1.

r and the regression slope

The slope of the regression line of weight on age (the kilograms gained per month of age, built in §12.2) is b = r × s_y ÷ sₓ = 0.82 × 1.45 ÷ 7.91 = 0.150 kg/month. The two answer different questions. r is unit-free and symmetric: it measures how tightly the points hug a line. b has units and direction: it says how much y changes per unit of x. A shallow line with little scatter gives r near 1 and a small b. The t of 14.19 above is exactly the t that §12.2.4 obtains for b, because testing ρ = 0 and testing that the slope is zero ask the same question.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
cov(cl$age_months, cl$weight_kg)
cor.test(cl$age_months, cl$weight_kg)
[1] 9.379596

    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  cl$age_months and cl$weight_kg
t = 14.188, df = 98, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.7434410 0.8754941
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.8201033

cov returns the covariance (9.38 kg·months). cor.test prints r (0.82), the t statistic of step 3 with its 98 df, and the Fisher-z interval of step 4 (0.74 to 0.88).

blocks.alt: Scatter patterns at different correlation strengths
blocks.caption: Figure 11.2. Scatter patterns at different correlation strengths.

points.html: r² is the proportion of the variance in one variable that is accounted for by its linear relationship with the other. For age and weight, r² = 0.82² = 0.67: 67% of the variation in weight goes with age. It reappears as R² in §12.2.5.

Verbal labels for the size of r (“weak”, “moderate”, “strong”) are conventions and differ between authors. Mukaka (2012), for example, calls 0.2 “negligible” and 0.3 “low positive”. Report r with its confidence interval rather than a label alone.

The t-test and Fisher interval assume the pairs are independent and the two variables are jointly Normal (Schober et al., 2018). For skewed data, ordinal data or outliers, use a rank coefficient (§11.3).
r is sensitive to outliers because it is built from means and squared deviations. One extreme point can create or destroy a correlation. Look at the scatter diagram.

r depends on the range sampled. Restrict the clinic register to the 26 children aged 24–30 months and r falls from 0.82 to −0.02: over six months the age effect is small beside child-to-child scatter, although children still gain weight with age.
A significant r is not a large r. With n = 1,000, r = 0.07 gives p ≈ 0.03 but explains 0.5% of the variance.

r measures association, not agreement. Two methods of measuring blood pressure can correlate at 0.95 while one reads 10 mmHg higher than the other. Bland and Altman (1986) showed why correlation is misleading for method comparison; the right method (limits of agreement, built on the differences between the two readings) is taught in §16.3.5.
Correlations computed across groups (districts, states) need not hold for individuals: the ecological fallacy (recall §1.5).
